Chapter 2: Searching for a Clear Answer—What Does It Mean to Be Holy?
Have you ever noticed how, when someone asks what makes an action truly good or holy, most people just reach for whatever example pops into their mind? Maybe it’s a childhood story, a ritual they’ve watched a hundred times, or a rule they were told never to break. But when you push a little deeper—ask them to define what it really means to be holy in a way that always makes sense—suddenly, the answer isn’t so easy.
That’s exactly what played out between two men standing outside a courthouse. The older man, the type who’s never satisfied with just scratching the surface, turned to the younger and asked, “So, what does piety really mean?” Not just in this moment, but in a way that works no matter the situation.
The younger guy, feeling pretty sure of himself, gave an answer that seemed simple enough: piety is doing what the gods love.
At first, that sounds pretty reasonable, right? If the gods are the ultimate judges of right and wrong, then following what they love should lead to holiness. But the older man wasn’t convinced. He pointed out something we might all recognize—the stories about the gods are full of disagreements. One god loves something, another hates it. If piety is just about pleasing the gods, how could anyone ever be sure they’re on the right track?
The conversation got more intense. The younger man tried to clarify—maybe piety is about prosecuting wrongdoers, even if they’re family. But again, the older man pressed on. Is every act of justice holy, or just some? Is there more to being holy than holding people accountable? Over and over, the younger man found himself circling back to the same answer, unable to come up with a definition that fit every case.
What really came to light is that, when it comes to something as complex as holiness, most people just lean on examples. They know what feels right in the moment, but they struggle to explain why. The older man's questions exposed the limits of that way of thinking. Without a clear definition, how can you really know you’re doing the right thing? How can laws be just, or rituals have meaning, if you never fully understand their purpose?
And honestly, this isn’t just an ancient problem. Even now, we find ourselves stuck between what tradition tells us and what we can actually explain. That conversation outside the courthouse reminds us that the search for clarity isn’t always comfortable. It can feel awkward, even frustrating, to realize we don’t have all the answers. But that discomfort? It’s necessary. Without it, our beliefs stay untested, and our actions can start to feel empty.
As their exchange went on, it became obvious: the journey toward understanding is rarely a straight line. Every answer sparks new questions, and every moment of certainty opens the door to doubt. But in the middle of all that back-and-forth, something important was happening. The younger man, even though he was frustrated, was being challenged to think deeper than ever before. And the older, despite his own worries, was showing what it looks like to keep searching for truth—to refuse to settle for easy answers.
